He then sent a telegram to the office of the Secretary of State, and in the afternoon received a reply stating that the government would do nothing in the matter. I believe that this is a very serious position for any government to be placed m, to send out forms such as I have in my band, from which the bribery clauses have been entirely omitted.
And I might say further that I urged the returning officer to insist on having these clauses in the form sent to the deputy returning officers throughout the country. He refused to do it, stating that the form the government sent him was the one that would be used and that he had already sent them out to the deputy returning officers And I certainly believe that this is a matter of vital importance not only to the people in the ridings in which elections are being held to-day, but to the whole country I understand that in the last Dominion eiee-timi these were the forms used in many different parts of the country. I certainly believe that if this is the manner in which the people of the province are to be treated, il only part of the oath is to be placed in the form to be used, I cannot help but see that it is a scheme, on the part of the government, might I say, to take advantage of

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must inform the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) and the House that this is the first information I have received of anything of the kind suggested by him in his remarks. The Secretary of State has not communicated with me on the subject. Had the hon. gentleman given me notice of his intention to bring the matter forward, I would have informed myself with regard to it. He says- or rather, he insinuates-that there has been a conspiracy on the part of the government to deprive the electors of their rights. I must tell the hon. gentleman that this language is absolutely uncalled for and unwarranted-there has been no conspiracy of the kind. I never heard of the matter until this moment. I can hardly be expected, under the circumstances, to give the hon. gentleman information as to the papers sent by the Secretary of State to the returning officers. But I am sure that nothing unusual has been done, but that the regular course has been followed. Had I been informed by the hon. gentleman that he intended to'make such a statement as he has made, I would have made It my duty to call upon the Secretary of State to ascertain what had actually been done. But I am sure that nothing has been done by the Secretary of State that is not according to the law, and I hasten to repel the insinuation of the hon. gentleman that In the election there has been any difference in the form sent out in one county from that sent out in others. All the forms were the same; cither all were right or all were wrong. It is not fair to the government, it would not be fair to anybody, that such grave insinuations should be made when the hon. gentleman who makes them had the opportunity at once to call the attention of the government to the matter and receive an explanation. It is not possible now for me to give any answer to the hon. gentleman except to say that my old colleague, my venerable colleague, the Secretary of State is incapable of doing such a thing as has been insinuated against him. Hon. Mr. Scott is an old man, a respectable man if there is one in the country, a man now approaching fourscore years. It is not fair to him to insinuate against him that in his old age he would be guilty of such an act as has been suggested. It is probably like the telegram of Mr. Cousins of Medicine Hat;- when we have the full information before us, it will probably be found another roorback.

speechtext:
The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) does not seem to feel indignation that the plain provisions of the statute have been
violated, not only in the elections now going on, but in the general elections of November last. But, that a matter of this kind should be mentioned even in what seemed to me, the moderate terms used by my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) seemed to excite the right hon. gentleman to grave and indignant rebuke.
I should have thought that there might be some room for indignation in the mind of my right hon. friend that the statute had been violated, that an act had been committed, which, if committed wilfully, I suppose would render some one liable to indictment under the common laws of England for malfeasance in office. I am not saying that it was done wilfully. But I have heard from a number of my friends on this side that exactly the same thing was perpetrated in the last general election, and with somewhat extraordinarv results. I am told that in one riding the oath was taken in the mutilated form for a time, but after the deputy returning officer had been informed that he was to modify the oath sent out by the administration o'f which the right hon. gentleman is the head, the result was that it was not taken in that form by certain electors. I have before me, handed to me by my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), the form of oath which was sent out by this government. I do not care whether the Secretary of State sent it out or what member of the government did so. My right hon. friend is responsible for sending it out, for he is the head of the administration ; and every gentleman who sits on those treasury benches is responsible for this violation of the statute, which I am assuming is not wilful, but which certainly merits investigation and discussion in this parliament and in this country.
Now, what are the circumstances 1 By section 65 of the Dominion Elections Act, the oath which is used in the province must be used in Dominion elections. These provisions of the statute are quite distinct, and I will not trouble the House by reading it, for my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) drafted these provisions, and no doubt, has them in mind as well as the debate that took place when this statute was enacted by this parliament. We are referred, therefore, to the oath in use in Ontario, in order to ascertain the proper form of oath to be submitted to electors in these by-elections, for the form of oath in use in the province must be used in Dominion elections with certain modifications which are not material for this purpose.
In Ontario we find this ' Form 16 ' which I exhibit to the House and which bears this title :	' Ontario Form 16. Form of Oath
in ordinary cases to be administered at an election to a voter by virtue of manhood suffrage, made applicable to Dominion elections.' Now we come down to the Ontario statute, and we ascertain whether or

not this form corresponds with that known as ' Form 16 ' in that statute. Perhaps in order to make the matter perfectly plain I had better read the whole document:

Ontario Act, section 98. Dominion Elections Act, 1900, sections 21 and 65 :

I think this is a subject which has been before the House one way or another during the present session, because my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) moved for all these forms, and if I am not mistaken some reference was made to this circumstance either by him or by some other hon. gentleman. At all events my hon. friend from Hamilton brought it to the attention of the House by moving for the forms. I think that when two of the most important clauses of the oath are omitted from a document sent out to the returning officers throughout this country only a few days ago, when these two clauses are omitted from a document prepared by this government and for which document my right hon. friend the leader of the government is as much responsible as any one of his colleagues, we require something more than a mere airy rebuke to my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) for mentioning this matter. Does not my right hon. friend think that when a returning officer, at the instance of my hon. friend from Lambton, brings the matter, both by telephone and telegraph, to the attention of this government on the day before the election, some other answer should be given to that returning officer than that this is a matter in which the government cannot interfere and in which nothing will be done. Conservatives not only in these elections, but during the general elections in November last were compelled to go to the trouble themselves, as far as possible, of bringing the provisions of the law to the attention of the deputy returning officers. I am bound to suppose, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that this is a mere oversight, but it is a most remarkable oversight, as I think my right hon. friend himself will admit. For what possible reason, under what possible misapprehension could a department of this government, having a trained and competent staff, venture to prepare a document of that kind leaving out two clauses, the omission of which may he made to answer a certain purpose which would not be a very creditable purpose, I am sure. Under what circumstances could this have arisen ? Have the government been in ignorance during the last four or five months of the character of the document which they sent out during the last general election, a document which was used, as I understand it, not only in the province of Ontario, but in the province of Quebec as my hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) informs me ? It seems to me a most remarkable thing, if the circumstance is as stated by my hon. friend from Beauharnois, that the bribery clauses of the Ontario oath should not only have been omitted, but that the bribery clauses of the oath according to the provincial laws of Quebec should also have been omitted from the form sent into that province. You might understand how one

mistake might be made in regard to a particular province, in regard to the province of Ontario, but will my right hon. friend or any member of his government inform me how it should happen that the bribery clauses of the oath in other provinces have been omitted ? X must confess I cannot understand it for the present and I venture to hope that my right hon. friend will, if he is not able to do so to-day, on some future occasion, give to the House some further explanation than that which he has vouchsafed this afternoon. ,

speechtext:
What is the matter with hon. gentlemen opposite? Something seems to have struck the risible nerve of my hon. friend there and he cannot contain himself. In 1900, the government of which my right hon. friend is head, and of which the present Minister of Justice was the Minister of Justice then, made this up and in that form which purported to be form 16 of the Ontario Act they gave an exact rescript of that form in which appeared these two sections which were omitted from the next form :
(8)	That you have not received anything, nor has anything been promised you, either directly or indirectly in order to induce you to vote at this election or for loss of time, travelling expenses, hire of teams or any other service connected therewith.
(9)	And that you have not directly or indirectly paid or promised anything to any person in order to induce him to vote or refraim from voting at the election.



That was the form issued by the government in the year 1900, and under the Secretary of State who is in office to-day. Why the change? Now, when we come to the by-election for 1905-I am not speaking of the general elections now for I have not the form before me-what do you find? There is the same assertion at the top that this is No. 10 of the Ontario Act oath to be administered, and a lie at the bottom of it. Who was it that authorized the lie ? Who was it that deceived the people of this country and every deputy returning .officer and every voter, by saying to him as he came to vote: this is the oath that the Ontario statute provides for; this is all you need take so far as, the Ontario law is concerned; and then excise two principal clauses from that oath in so far as bribery and corruption are concerned. Who did it? It was not my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden); it was not even my bold and audacious friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) so lacking in courtesy as to dare to bring up at this hour in parliament a thing of such a shameless and glaring kind as this. A conspiracy, said my right hon. friend. Who charges a conspiracy ? He may talk conspiracy if lie likes, but he has got to acknowledge utter and crass neglect or something worse on the part of the department which once knew what was right and *did it, and which next election knew what was right and did wrong. That is just as bad as conspiracy. I say that whether there was design or not, there is the plain fact: there are the two instructions, one of 1900 and one of 1905; there is the statute of Ontario which has the oath out of which the principal parts have been excised by the Secretary of State of the government of which my" right hon. friend is the head and of which the Minister of Justice is now and was then the Minister of Justice. In the general elections last fall, when hon. gentlemen opposite were using evex-y kind of influence they could; when they exercised their immense influence to draw sums of money from contributors right and left -and used it with the most lavish hand that was ever known in this Dominion of Canada, there was a reason why the bribery [DOT]oath should be left out. To-day there may be the same reason why the bribery oath should be left out. It is left out. It is not our fault it is left out. It was this government that left it out knowing what they should have put in, and doing what they should have done in 1900, but neglecting to do it to-day.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
For a number of years I have taken a very great interest in the election law. On a former occasion I introduced a Bill with the object of amending the Election Act, and as I thought improving that law. and I am happy to say that the suggestions I made then have since been embodied in the sta-Mr. FOSTER.
tute. This matter which at present is engaging the attention of the House was discussed by many of the newspapers in the province of Ontario on account of what they called the mutilated oath that was used in the Dominion elections. In order to have the subject brought before parliament the hon. gentleman from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) moved on the 15th of February that all the forms.used in the last Dominion election be laid on the table. They were laid on the table of the House, and* I took pains to verify the mutilated oath in these papers. The form of oath used in 1900 contained the anti-bribery clauses but at the last general election I was surprised to learn that clauses 8 and .9 were omitted from that oath. I thought it proper to prepare a form of oath and placed it in the hands of the scrutineers in my constituency so that if an elector should be sworn the proper oath should be administered. In some cases the deputy returning officer refused to administer any other oath than that forwarded to him by the government. In one instance, the returning officer persisted in having the oath administered in part, but at the expiration of an hour he concluded to administer the oath the scrutineer handed to him, and he did so for the balance of the day. The Minister of Justice is very careful that we should speak by the book and I shall do so. On the loth of February, the hon. member for Hamilton moved, for these papers and during the discussion on the Autouomv Bill I informed the Minister of Justice that I intended to bring up a matter in connection with his department. This very matter is the matter I then referred to. I did not expect it would be brought up to-day, but it would have been brought up before this were it not for the discussion on the Autonomy Bill. In order that I may do no injustice to the government, I shall state the absolute facts of the case as they are and I am prepared to stand by these facts as a member of this House. I have committed them to writing and I now give this statement to the House: For the past thirty years or more, in fact ever since the enactment of anti-bribery legislation, the ordinai-y form of election oath has always included what may be described as the standard anti-bribery clauses. The substance of these clauses is the sworn statement that the voter has not been bribed and that he has not bribed any one else. Every ordinai-y oath of qualification used in Ontario, not only in Dominion elections but in provincial and municipal elections as well, during all these years contained these clauses, till the last election when the form of oath printed and distributed for use by the Dominion officials for the first time, and without any change of law or circumstances whatever to justify it, unexpectedly and unaccountably left them out. It is well known that voters are often stopped from voting

by being confronted with the anti-bribery clauses, and scrutineers during all those years had only to ask for the administration of the oath and every one understood that that oath included anti-bribery clauses.
Why then were these clauses that had always heretofore been included, and which Conservative scrutineers and workers expected would still be included, quietly left out in 1901 ? Such a change, even if proper, should not have been made without special attention being called to it. But no notice whatever was given of it. Not even in the instructions to the returning officers or their deputies was there the slightest reference to it.
Any one familiar with the practical workings of matters at an election booth will understand how this omission of the bribery clauses would operate. It must be remembered that the election oath is not something that every voter has to take. No ordinary voter has to take the oath unless one of the scrutineers demands that he shall take it. The ordinary arrangements at a polling place are that the scrutineers are given a list of voters with certain names marked to be sworn. The scrutineer may or may not know the circumstances or reason why it is thought proper to swear a particular voter. His list is marked by the chairman or committee in charge of the division, usually on private and confidential information. The scrutineer depends on his marked list, and his duties are to watch the proceedings at the poll and swear the persons marked to be sworn. The instructions to the scrutineer always are to insist on the whole oath being put in each case so as to cover all grounds of objection, including bribery. The instructions to Conservative scrutineers last time were the same as usual, no one for a moment suspecting that the bribery clauses would not be included as they had always been in the ordinary form of oath. The government officials and deputy returning officers who had received the forms were the only persons that had a chance to know that these clauses were left out. Whether they discovered the fact before the election or not is a question. Some of them no doubt did but at any rate they kept it a secret from their political opponents. Unfortunately things have reached such a pass in our part of the country at least that the returning officers, deputies and clerks are, with a few exceptions, as much or almost as much partisans as the Liberal scrutineers. In the majority of cases, as things go now-a-days, the person appointed as deputy returning officer in a polling division is one of the most active Liberal workers of the division, often the chairman and nearly always a member of the Liberal committee of workers.
This was the state of affairs oh the morning of last 3rd of November when the poll opened. What would happen ? A voter would come in whom the Conservative scrutineer had instructions to swear. The scrutineer would ask to have him sworn, supposing as he and all the Conservative workers did that the ordinary oath contained the bribery clauses. The oath would be administered without the bribery clauses. In some cases perhaps no one would notice the omission, every one taking it for granted^ that the official oath was all right and in the usual form. If the Liberal deputy'did notice it there would be slim chances indeed that he would tell the Conservative scrutineer of it. If the Conservative scrutineer noticed it he might perhaps ask to look at the official form to see that it was read correctly, and when he was shown that it had been, unless he was an expert in election law, there was small chance of his having anything more to say. The device of administering two oaths in order to catch the anti-bribery clauses was something he had never before heard of. There is often too a repugnance on the part of scrutineers especially in country places to asking directly or specifically to have the bribery clauses administered to one of his neighbours. If he did speak of the bribery clauses he would be told by the deputy, as I am informed was actually done in a number of cases in Elgin, that that was the oath and all the oath that was supplied. In short the effect of the conduct of the government officials would be that no voter would have to swear either that he had not been bribed or that he had not bribed any one else unless the surreptitious omission of the bribery clauses was discovered and unless the means of remedying it were known to and insisted on by the scrutineer. As a matter of fact there were but very few cases in the province where the bribery clauses were administered.
And let me say in passing that I have inquired from other members from the province of Ontario oil this side of the House, and I find that the same thing existed in their parts of the province ; and I have no doubt since I examined the official documents laid on the table of the House, that the same form was used all over the province.
As I have said, even if the omission of these clauses from the oath was justified it should not have been done without attention being called to the change. Notice should have been given not only to the officials and deputies but also to the public or at any rate to the candidates on both sides. But, as I have before stated, not a word was said about it. Not even the deputies were notified of it. A perusal of the instructions to the returning officers will show that they were word for word the same in 1904 when the clauses were left out as they were in 1900 when they were in. I have them both here.
But there was no just cause whatever for leaving these anti-bribery clauses out. They were left in in 1900 and the sections of the Act prescnibing the oaths (sections 21 and 65) were precisely the same in 1900 as in 1904. Section 65 says ' that an elector if
7343

required shall take such oath of qualification as by the law of the province he may in the like case at a provincial election be required to take, such changes having been made in the form of oath as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held.' We have then to go to the Ontario Election Act (I have it here) and we find that the form [DOT]there prescribed (see section 98) in Form 16 in schedule ' A ' to that Act. This is the oath of qualification required by the provincial law. It contains the anti-bribery clauses (numbers 8 and 9) as all such oaths for more than a quarter of a century back have always contained them. This form 16 then is the oath of qualification which the Dominion Election Act prescribes. Yes, it will be said, but some changes in it are authorized by the above quoted provision of section 65. That is right, but note carefully what changes. Such changes and such only as ' are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held.' What then are these changes 1 Just what were made in 1900 and not one iota more-the omission from the end of the first clause of the oath the words * in the poll book,' because in the Dominion election the official list is not in the poll book, as it is in the provincial, but is a separate printed list. Not for one single instant can it be contended with the slightest show of reason that it was necessary to omit the anti-bribery clauses in order to make the provincial oath applicable to the Dominion election. These clauses are as strictly and as emphatically applicable as any other clause in the oath. The bribery aimed at by these clauses is forbidden by section 108 of the Dominion Act in the same terms as it is forbidden in the provincial Act. These omitted clauses word for word are in fact contained in Form ' R ' of the Dominion Act, showing if further proof were needed that they are not repugnant but are absolutely applicable to the Dominion elections. Moreover the oath of qualification Form S in the old Dominion Act. which the present provincial oath takes the place of contained these clauses in the same exact words. Neither in precedent nor in theory was there the slightest ground for leaving these anti-bribery clauses out. Why was it done ?
But there is still another and perhaps a more serious aspect of the case yet to be pointed out, and that is that this altered form which was printed and sent forth by the government officials purports to be what it is not. I have here one of the emasculated forms that was actually sent forth and used by the officials. While it omits the anti-bribery clauses it is so headed as to lead one to believe that it contained them. It is headed Form 16. Form 16 is a well known form and well known to contain these anti-bribery clauses. What is sent forth as Form 16 is not the genuine Form 16 at all, but a false, mutilated and misleading form. Just look at it and compare it with the genuine form in Mr. INGRAM.
the Ontario Election Act or with the form actually used by the government in 1900 (I have them both here) and see what a deception and a fi'aud it is. Its heading also states that it is the form of oath for use in ordinary cases and this leads to the supposition that it is the only and all the oath applicable to such cases. If it was intended merely to be supplemental to another oath, or another oath to it, why did it not state so on the face of it either in the heading or in a foot note ?
From whatever point of view we regard it, this oath matter is utterly indefensible.
The foregoing is the position of the case in brief. It is an absolutely correct and unassailable presentation of the facts and circumstances of the matter. But some excuses are attempted.
It is said that Form 16 is not an oath of qualification, that only part of it, namely the part without the bribery clauses is what is meant in section 65 by ' oath of qualification.' There is nothing in such a contention. For thirty years and more all ordinary oaths of qualification used at elections contained these anti-bribery clauses. Form S and Form X in the old Act (which I have here) which are headed and called oaths of qualification contain these identical clauses. This very Form 16 of the Ontario Election Act, and the whole of it, is described and referred to in the Ontario Election Act itself as ' the oath of qualification.' (See section 94, subsection 5 of Ontario Election Act). It is mere twaddle to pretend that the whole of Form 16 is not what is referred to and intended in section 65 as the oath of qualification. And section 65 justifies no omissions from it whatever. Any changes necessary to make it applicable to Dominion Elections are authorized. That might mean that if the anti-bribery clauses were not properly or appropriately worded for Dominion Elections the wording might be changed, but in no wise could it mean that these clauses were to be wholly left out.
Again it is said that because anti-bribery clauses are contained in Form 'U,' and Form ' U ' might be administered, therefore it was right to leave the bribery clauses out of Form 16-in other words that Form 'TJ' and Form 1C were merely supplemental to each other and that one was not intended to contain anything that the other contained.
Such a contention is altogether wrong, even apart from the fact that the mutilation of Form 16 would, even on such a ground, be a direct violation of the provisions of section 65. Form ' U ' has a primary and direct purpose of its own namely to head off persons who are disfranchised by reason of having been found guilty of bribery or corrupt practices at some former election. Peruse section 7 of the Dominion Election Act, and the Act and sections referred to in section 7 and this will be abundantly clear.
Moreover the official who prepared the

mutilated oath did not proceed on the ground that nothing must be duplicated In the two oaths. I want the right bon. gentleman to mark this. If he had he would have left out not only the bribery clauses (8 and 9) but also clause 7 (as to not having voted before) which, unlike the bribery clauses, is retained in the mutilated form though it is also in Form ' U.'
Excuse is also attempted for departure from the course that was followed in 1900 of leaving the bribery clauses in, by pointing out that there had been in 1900 a clerical error in the heading of Form 'U' which was corrected in 1901. That could in no view be any justification for the change, and if the state of the heading furnished any reason at all one way or the other, the condition it was left in in 1904 made it more necessary to have Form 16 complete in itself then than in 1900. For the erroneous heading was corrected before the elections of 1900, by official instructions from the Department of the Secretary of State, dated 12tli October, 1900, directing the deputy returning officers to ' absolutely ignore ' that erroneous heading as it was inserted by mistake. I have here this official instruction ; it is pasted right to this Form * XJ.' The heading as it now stands and as it stood in 1904 indicates that the oath Form 'U' is intended for a special class of persons and not for general or ordinary cases, while as it was in 1900 with the official instructions to ignore the heading altogether it might be inferred that it was for general and ordinary use. The fact also that a special instruction was issued in 1900 regarding it would specially draw attention to the fact that there was such an oath and that it was expected it would be used.
Never before was it necessary to administer any additional oath besides the ordinary one in order to catch a voter on bribery.
If the oath Form ' D ' had even been printed and distributed like Form 16 it would have made things a little less objectionable.
If the law does not require the antibribery clauses to be inserted or rather left in Form 16, and if it was proper to send that mutilated oatli forth without them, then there was a time (from 1898 to I960) when no anti-bribery clauses could be administered to a voter at all. The preseut section 65 upon which the matter under discussion hangs is, so far as it relates to the oath in question, taken word for word from section 45, subsection 2 of the 1898 Act ; and this was the only oath which could under the 1898 Act be administered to a voter. Can it be supposed that it ever was the intention that no voter should be sworn as to bribery?
Wholly unjustified, false, mutilated and misleading is the fitting characterization of the thing that was sent forth and used as the official form of oath at the last Dominion election.
I make this statement to the House, and it is a statement of the facts in connection
with this mutilated form of oath. Why that was done, I cannot understand. There was no justification for it. There is no amendment to the Act which necessitated it; and whoever did it, did it with a purpose. Will my right hon. friend pretend to say that all the deputy returning officers throughout Canada, who were furnished the election documents which were laid on the table of this House, were sufficiently well posted in the Election Act of Canada to choose, when a scrutineer asked one of them to swear a voter, from the three separate oaths which one they should administer ? Would any hon. gentleman pretend to say that ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Pretend to say what.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: That if, an elector going into his polling booth, the scrutineer of either party asking the returning officer to swear him, any deputy returning officer would be sufficiently well posted in the election law to take out of three different oaths make a complete oath to administer to the elector ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I do not know that our deputy returning officers in British Columbia are any more intelligent than those in other parts of Canada ; but I remember being in a polling booth, when the deputy returning officer asked the scrutineer : Which oath do you want administered-the qualification oath or the bribery oath ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Your election law in British Columbia is different from ours ; but speaking for the province of Ontario, I have stated exactly what occurred, and I say there was no justification for amending the oath and making it any different from what it was in 1900. Then it was a correct oath, and any deputy returning officer administering it, would be administering the oath in full. I want to point out in addition that the first oath was a correct and a convenient form, why therefore should it have been mutilated and the bribery clauses struck out ? There was no justification for that, nor was there any change in the election Act which required a change in the oath at all. That is where the government made a mistake, or an. official of the government mutilated the oath which was required to be administered.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
Like my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, I do not wish to imply that this was done in that particular case with design, but the circumstances are rather extraordinary and so is the coincidence ; because, as my hon. friend has said, the very same thing was done during the last election in the province of Quebec. I had not examined the papers which were in the polling booth, when my attention was called to the matter in Valleylield, where there Is a very large vote. Let me read to

the House the oath that was there given to the elector. This is the English form of the oath prescribed by section 143 of the Quebec Election Act, 1903, made applicable to Dominion elections pursuant to the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, 1900, in that behalf. This is the oath :
5Tou swear (or affirm, as the case may be), ta answer the truth and nothing but the truth to the questions which will be put to you ; so help you God.
1.	Are you the person meant or Intended to be meant by the name entered as follows (name of the elector entered on the list) on the list of electors for this polling division ?
2.	Are you a subject of His Majesty ?
3.	Have you been naturalized in any other country or taken thereto the oath of allegiance?
4.	Are you of the full age of twenty-one years ?
5.	Have you voted before to-day at this election, for this electoral district, at this or any other polling station ?
8. Not being a proprietor and residing out of Canada for over a year, have you returned to this country with your family, at least one month before the election with the intention of remaining therein ?
That is the oath that was administered to the voters in the county of Beauharuois at the last general election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: The matter is absolutely new to me and I desire information. The hon. member says that this is the form of oath administered in the Beauliar-nois election. Was there not another oath against bribery ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
Not at all. When my attention was called to it-we know what is done during elections, we know how fidgety our friends are. and when they came to me and said : ' This is an extraordinary oath ; there is nothing at all in that, and we want to get-the oath which should be given to the electors, ' I went to the poll and saw the deputy and asked him if he had not any other form of oath. He said : No. I said : That is nothing. He said : This is the oath I found among my papers, and it is the one I am going to administer. I asked for the Act, and 'although I had not the local Act in my pocket, I took the Dominion Elections Act and showed him clause 05. I have found that in my province the officials on election day are generally our most bitter opponents. X do not say they are dishonest, but they will not listen to anything, they pretend to stand by their duty, and when a man says :1 This is what I found in the box and I will not use anything else but that,' I cannot tell that man he is dishonest, although I know he is a bitter opponent of mine and has been working against me. I read clause 65 of the Act, which is as follows :
_ An elector, if required by the deputy returning officer, the poll clerk, one of the candidates, or an agent of a candidate or by any elector present shall, before receiving his ballot paper, Mr. BERGERON.
take such oath of qualification as by the Jaw of the province he may in the like case at a provincial election be required to take, such changes having^ been made in the form of oath as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held, and shall also, if so required, take 'the oath in the form ' U.'
Now, what is the form of oath used ? It is very much a repetition of this for the first paragraphs, but this is what is essential, and I imagine that is why it was drawn in this form. This is the form :
That you have not received anything, that you do not expect anything, nor has anything been promised you directly or indircetly, to induce you to vote at this election, either for loss of time, travelling .expenses, hire of team, or for any other service, connected therewith.
That you have not, directly or indirectly, paid or promised anything to any person either to induce him to vote or to refrain from voting at this election.
That you are not otherwise disqualified from voting at this election.
So help you God.
I asked the deputy returning officer In the poll at which I was to add these words to the oath he was taking from the elector. There is not a man in this House who will say it was not the Intention of the legislature that the two oaths should he given. The deputy returning officer refused to do so. although I showed him the law. He said: " Mr. Bergeron, I have nothing to do with that ; X have received instructions to put this oath." And he did not do it.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Was not the returning officer supplied with a copy of the Election Act in the box ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I took the Dominion Electoral Act in the poll and showed it to him, but how could I force him to administer the oath ? The consequence was that in every poll in Valleyfield I could not get any other oath administered but this. I do not say it was done intentionally. I do not want to imply that the government have done that intentionally, but it is a most estraordinary thing that it should be done first in our province and now in the province of Ontario. Would it not be better, and avoid mistakes, if, since we are obliged by law to take the oath of the local Act and apply the federal Act to it, we should have a printed form of the local Act, the whole Act as it is in the local and in the Dominion Acts, and then there would be no mistake ? I only mention this matter, because we have been talking about it in connection with the other case. In my county I found in every poll that I could not obtain from the deputy returning officer what the law required. He had no instructions to that effect, and he would not comply with the law as passed by this parliament.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice has complained that this question is. 'sprung upon him without reasonable notice. I wish to confirm what lias been
said already from this side, that there was no intention to spring this subject at ail.
It would not have been brought up for some da vs to come had It not been for the extraordinary conduct of the government in respect to the pending election in Oxford. I understand that a complaint was made in Woodstock about the form being used, and a telegram was sent to the government asking instructions, and I am told-the right hon. gentleman can tell me whether I am right or wrong-that the government s answer was to stand by the forms sent and no others. Under these circumstances, we on this side thought it our duty immediately to bring these questions up. I personally would have preferred to have the discussion later, because I have not papers here which I intended to use when this subject would come up ; but as it is now, we may as well discuss the whole matter. It has been said b' hon. gentlemen opposite that this is a mistake of the Clerk of the Crown in Qhan- , eerv. I contend that it is nothing of the kind. These instructions are the instructions of the government issued by the Clerk 0f the Crown, but subject to the approval ot tlie Governor in Council, and the government is directly responsible for the instructions issued. Section 21 of the Dominion Elections Act provides this :
Immediately after the issue of the writ of election the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall transmit to the returning officer a sufficient number of copies of voters lists, if there are any, one copy of this Act, and of such instructions approved by the Governor in Council as are required to carry out the election according to the provisions of this Act.
Therefore, Sir, the instructions which we are discussing are not, strictly speaking, instructions of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, but instructions approved ana adopted by the government. Same clause goes on :
The instructions referred to in subsection 1 of this section contain forms of the oaths referred to in sections 65, 66 and 68.
The instructions shall contain the forms of the oaths in sections 65, GG and G8. Let us see what section 65 says ?
The elector, if required by the deputy returning officer, the polling clerk, one of the candidates, or any agent of the candidates, or by any elector present shall, before receiving the ballot paper, take such oath of qualification as by the law of the province he may in the like case at a provincial election be required to take.
That form shall be part of the instructions. In November, 1904, or in the present by-elections, what form was given in connection with the provincial law ? The statute does not say part of the provincial form, but the whole of the form.
Take such oath of qualification as by the law of the province he may in a like case at a provincial election he required to take, such changes having been made in the form of oath
as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held.
Of course some of the words have to be changed ; the provincial election had to be made the Dominion election, and so on.
And shall also, if so required, take the o'atlx in the form * U.'
If so required. If not required to take the form 1 U,' is he only to take part of the provincial oath. Surely, if the candidate or an elector did not call upon the form ' U ' to be sworn to, the oath called for in section 65 was the whole provincial oath ? To say that the provincial oath was to be supplemented by form ' U ' is it seems to me, an absurd reading of that section. But if we take the Quebec form read by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) we *will see the utter absurdity of that contention. Take the form issued in November last by the Dominion government for the elections in Quebec together with form U and administer both of them to an elector,, and you will not comply with the law. There is more in the province of Quebec affidavit than you will find in the form issued by the government and form ' U ' put together. The Quebec Election Act, 1903, chapter 9, section 143, has what may be called the bribery clauses in the form of questions. It is in this form :
Has any promise been made to you or to your wife or to any of your relations, friends or other persons, to induce you to vote or not to vote at this election ?
Neither in the form issued by the government or in form 1 U ' are the words or not to vote.' And who will say that thisi is not a very material part of the oath ? Why, it is a very common practice among certain people who run what is called the machine in the various provinces, to pay a man not to vote. A man does that by perhaps spoil ing his ballot or putting in a blank ballot, and in the province of Quebec he can be sworn that he has not received anything not to vote.
Have you received anything, either personally or through your wife, or through any member of vour family, or in any other manner to induce you to vote or not to vote at this election, or in relation to your vote at this election .
There are no such words to be found itr the form issued by the government or in the form 'IJ.'
Have vou been guilty of or participated in any corrupt practice whatever which disqualifies, you from taking part in this election .
That goes further than form ' U.' Form 'IT' is an affidavit that he has not been convicted, and this not only reaches the man that has been convicted, but the man who has been guilty and not convicted. The Dominion government substituted for this Act in the province of Quebec, two clauses neither of which cover this clause. I take it that that knocks from under the feet or

the government the contention that section 5 allowed ' U ' to be substituted for part of the provincial oath and the ground that had covered it for both together cannot cover it in the province of Quebec. Take the form read by my hon. friend from Beauharnois and add to that the form ' U ' and you do not get the provincial law. In the law of JNova Scotia there are the same bribery clauses, but of course in different terms, and the same thing applies to the election law of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island which has special forms of bribery clauses. The form of the bribery clauses in each province differs. And vet with regard to the elections in each province the bribery clause is struck out, with one exception and it is rather a curious one. The only form of affidavit in the Dominion in the November elections that had the bribery oath was that used in the Northwest Territories. Why the government thought the Northwest Territories required it I do not know, but that is the fact. Now with regard to what occurred in Hamilton as in other places ; after some hours of polling some of my friends in Hamilton discovered that this mutilated form of affidavit was being used. The gen-[DOT] tleinan who was acting as returning officer, a lawyer and a very honourable man, the moment his attention was called to it, he issued instructions to all the deputy returning officers to correct the form. He had not the slightest shadow of a doubt what his duty was and he complied with it immediately, and I found by an examination of the polling returns afterwards something which convinced me that the change in the form of the oath had done good. In East Hamilton we had a system of checking by our agents which amounted to the agent keeping a duplicate of the poll clerks' book, so that every agent knew the order in which every man voted, and he had each marked '* sworn ' or ' refused ' and so on. After the election I took some trouble to go over many of the polling divisions and I found that up to a certain point man after man who had been marked in the canvassing books to be sworn by our side took the oath. But after a certain time we found refusal after refusal by men who' were tendered the oath.
I cannot say absolutely that the first men knew that they were not to be subjected to the bribery oath, but the result did seem to lead to that conclusion.
I know that throughout the city men who wore interested in these things pointed out that they could not control the elections without that bribery oath and they were convinced that it was known broadcast throughout the city that there was no bribery oath in the form. I have no doubt at all that in cities, at all events, where the news would go pretty quickly, it would have a most serious effect upon any man's election to let it go forth that the people could get their votes in without anv fear of having the bribery oath administered. There is no doubt about that. Every one Mr. BARKER.
knows that is the case in cities where news gets around quickly. Then, what is the case in a county? It is utterly hopeless when a thing of that kind occurs for any man to correct anything wrong in the form it lie does And it out. In a county it would be absolutely impossible to send out new forms to all the polling divisions and have the matter corrected. The mischief is done and it cannot be remedied. Fortunately in the city of Hamilton we were able to se-because, having a good honest returning officer, he was very prompt in correcting it. But, the extraordinary thing, as has been pointed out here, is this: Having the printed form used in 1900 following strictly the provincial Act to go by, these officers like all other officers, repeat their forms; they do not go through the form of redrawing them. They have printed forms and they [DOT] use them over again. How was it that clauses 8 and 9 were struck out of that affidavit? What object could there be in striking them out? Surely it must have been plain to any man that the striking of the bribery clauses mate th*t affidavit was a most serious m/"el' and 1 cannot believe that the clerk of the Crown in Chancery or any other official would have dared to have taken out these clauses without authority. I cannot believe that he would have taken these clauses out and then have submitted the torm to the Governor in Council without having called attention to the omission or that experienced politicians like those sitting around the Council Board would not have thought that there was something extraordinary in striking these clauses out of the affidavits in the forms which had been already used.
I want to say one word more on this subject, not quite relating to the forms of the affidavit, but bearing upon the manner in which the government issues its writs to the returning officers conducting these elections. I intended to bring this [DOT].subject up on a future occasion, but I shall do so now
the mattei' In	Hamilton,
. gentteman who was appointed returning officer and who, I repeat, is a most respectable man-I have not a word to say against him, I have no suspicion of his conduct, I believe he is a perfectly honourable and straightforward man and that lie did his duty-was a junior partner in the firm of Chisholm and Doggie, the senior partner iu which was the president of the Reform Association of the city of Hamilton one of the most active men at the headquarters of the Liberal Association up to the time of the election and during polling day Not only that, but the firm of Chisholm & Doggie, carrying on business as lawyers, have, as most lawyers have, a vault common to the firm and open to the clerks in the office The ballot boxes, after the poll, were re-tuined to that office and kept in the vault ot that firm for three or four days. The

keys of this vault were not carried around j by the returning officer in his pocket-some thirty keys-but they were in charge of the clerks of the office. For three or four days these ballot boxes were practically under the control of the president of the Reform Association of Hamilton after the election. I am not finding fault with the returning officer. I am quite satisfied that he would do nothing wrong or be a party to anything wrong, but I do say it is an outrage that the government should have appointed a returning officer to carry on an election of that kind knowing, as the government must have known, that the papers and the ballot boxes after the election were under the control of my opponent just as much as they were under the control of the returning officer.

speechtext:
I'. DEMERS (St. .John and Iberville). Mr. Speaker, I think the argument presented by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) must have convinced the House that there was good reason for tne change in the form of the oath which was sent out. As most hon. members know the law is not the same in all the provinces and the laws of the provinces are not the same as the laws of the Dominion. We are by section 65 of the Dominion Act, permitted to use the forms of the provinces. Does that mean that we introduced into our law a provision admitting all the disabilities of the provinces? Not at all. All those which agree with our laws are admitted and that- is why, in section 65. we say that it shall be permitted to us to change the provincial form. For what reason do we change the provincial form? I will take the instance which has been given by the hon. member for Hamilton. In the province of Quebec it is settled by law that a man who has been proven guilty of bribery is disqualified from voting. Under our Dominion law it is a doubtful question, if I do not mistake. Then, was there not a good reason for a change in the form of that province? This disqualification, I maintain, which we have put into our provincial law could not be introduced into our Dominion law by a form of oath administered under the provincial law. It was not the intention of this parliament to disqualify electors who were disqualified by the provinces. I do not see anything to laugh at in my argument.
Mr. TISDALE, If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Demers) thinks I was laughing he is mistaken.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
This is a serious argument. It was not the intention to disqualify7 electors who are not disqualified under our law. This being the fact it was a sufficient reason for changing the form of oath of the province which change is authorized by section 65. I go further. Hon. gentlemen opposite may make a great noise
about this question but if they have the practical side of the question they have not the common sense nor logical sense. According to their contention we should have sworn these people twice for the same thing. It would not have been enough that the oath should have been administered according to our federal law, but we should have been obliged to have come under the local laws and to have sworn them twice. Would it be practicable to have the people sworn twice?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. gentleman what oath ' U ' is intended to
cover ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: It is because oath ' U ' is not useless, it is because the government had the right to make changes in the oath of the provinces that we have made the provision of section 65 that any voter, before being allowed to vote, shall be obliged to take the oath in Form ' U.' My hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) says that one officer refused that. His duty was plain. If so that officer was acting in bad faith and the party aggrieved had a right of action against him, but I do not believe that all over his county all of the officers understood their duty in the same way.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend (Mr. Demers) allow me one question ? Why have only half of the provincial oath in this form? Why not have the whole thing there so as to avoid any officer refusing to comply with the Dominion Election Act or refusing to administer the oath according to the Form ' U.' I am reading from the statutes of the province of Quebec, four paragraphs which have been omitted in this form which are nearly identical with the Btorm ' U ' of the Dominion Elections Act. Why was not the whole form put in of oath to be administered to the voters ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I say we have a law here which is our law. By section 65 we do not intend to bring up in our elections all the reasons of disqualifications of the provinces, but we only intend to cover those causes of disqualification' covered by our law. If you have disqualification for a certain Act under your Quebec law, it does not follow that the man is disqualified from voting under the Dominion law. Of course, he may incur a penalty, but if there is no disqualification under the federal law, do you think it is the intention of section 65 to disqualify him from voting, I say no. I say that section 65 is there for the purpose of permitting us to retain that part of the local laws which is necessary. And it is for this very reason that it has ben put in words so plain, under section. 65, that the Form ' U ' shall be used.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman means 64.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: No. 65. And section 68 says that no voter can receive a ballot if he refuses to take the oath in the Form ' U.'

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: But if the returning officer will not offer it ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: He will have to do it.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
But he does not.
Mi-. L. P. DEMERS. I cannot accept the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron)-

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. gentleman (Mr. L. P. Demers) will not take my word for it, because this happened to myself.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Then, why did not my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) prosecute the officer ? The case was a clear one. The law declares that no voter may have a ballot who refuses to take the oath according to the Form ' U.'

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: But if the form of oatli is changed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

My point was that section 65 requires the two oaths, one the oath of qualifications as required by the law of the province, changes being made in the form of the oath such as are necessary under our Dominion law and in addition to that the oath in the Form ' U.' Now what is the qualification of a voter. The qualification of a voter is prescribed by section 6 of the Franchise Act. Section 6 provides that:
No person possessed of the qualifications generally required by the provincial law to entitle him to vote at a provincial election, shall he disqualified from voting at a Dominion election merely by reason of any provision of the provincial law disqualifying from having his name on the list or from voting-
So that if a man is disqualified under the Provincial Act by reason of some act of bribery, he is not disqualified ns a result to vote under the Federal Act, and section 6 is the section which covers the point that a voter is entitled to vote and cannot be deprived of his right to vote because of some disqualification which is peculiar to the provincial Act, and as a result the oath of qualification required by the provincial law must be amended so as to cover the provisions of section 6 of the Franchise Act. But with respect to the bribery clauses this provision is contained in the form which is supplied to the returning officer, which form constitutes part of the Election. Act

and which hi's instructions say he must deliver in that form, assuming as the hon. member for St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers) argued a moment ago, that the provisions of the Dominion Election Act were different with respect to disqualification from the provisions of the provincial Act which, should supersede the other, could a voter be called upon to take an oath which would require him to be placed in contradiction under the Dominion Act to what he would swear to under the provincial Act. Is it proper that with respect to disqualification for bribery, two oaths should be put different iu words and different in substance V My argument is that section 65 of the "federal Act, properly construed, requires simply that the oath of qualification, which is the oath to be adapted from the provincial Act, should be sent out in a special form and the oath with respect to bribery in the Form ' U ' be administered in the form given in the Act.

It seems to me that the refutation of the arguments of the Minister of Inland Revenue and the Minister of Justice is contained in section 7 of form 16. Section 7 says :
That you have not voted before at this election, either at this or any other polling station.
The Minister of Justice contended that the old form sent out in 1900, the form which contained the full oath, was adopted in mistake on the part of the department, under that form when the bribery oath was required to be put to an elector it could be put and there was the form before the ic-turning officer, and there could be no such question as that which arose in Beauharnois. because it contained all the disqualifications as well- but here we have this oath which is set forth by the Minister of Justice as being the only right and correct thing and ft contains the very same objection as that contained in the- old instructions of 1900. maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.

If you have a right to have a portion of the disqualification in an oath you have a right

to have the whole thing in that oath, and I cannqt quite agree with the hon. gentlemen who have spoken - from this side of the House who have, so far as I have heard, said that they disclaim the idea that the government have wilfully done this thing.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.

It is done for a purpose I believe as firmly as I believe anything. I have listened to the arguments and I have' listened with considerable amusement to the Minister of Inland Revenue floundering in his argument Usually he is very clear, but he had such a bad case that he floundered badly in this instance. The Minister of Justice stated' bad law in order to try and bolster up a bad case, and from all these things I am perfectlv convinced that this is done wilfully, done for the purpose of making it difficult for justice to be done and for an honest vote to be cast, because the hon. gentlemen know perfectly that in these two elections to-day, if an honest vote of these two constituencies were cast, the government candidates would certainly be very badly defeated.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
When I spoke approvingly of the statement of my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Fowler) that these forms were sent out with malice aforethought, I heard from the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) a very loud Ha. Ha! as though my approving of that utterance afforded him amusement. Well, we have a right to take that view, considering the telegrams that have been read and that are now on * Hansard,' from the returning officer-not from the deputy returning officer-in North Oxford, and from ' the government in reply. The returning officer's telegram sounded much as if he were determined not to use any other forms than those supplied by the government. He telegraphed to the government for information, saying that the Conservatives were claiming that the form of oath should contain sections 8 and 9 of the provincial form and that he should get others printed to replace those that the government had sent him. Then, though he asked for instructions he as good as said these were the only forms he proposed to use. And the government telegraphed him back to engage a lawyer to interpret the instructions given to him. In the general elections of 1904, the same forms were supplied to the deputy returning officers in the province of Ontario. And in my own constituency I know of two cases where the deputy returning officer refused to put any other oafti than that furnished in form
10.	One was the case of a man working for myself. I found that he was going to drive away out in the country and vote and also that he had been paid by the secretary of the Reform Association ; that a horse had been furnished him and a man put in his place to work for him. I telegraphed Mr. John R. Dargavel. The hon. member for Brockville (Mr. Derbyshire) knows Mr. Dargavel and knows that he is as honest a man as there is in the country. Mr. Dargavel was acting as scrutineer at the poll at which this man proposed to vote. When the man filed an appearance Mr. Dargavel asked to have this man sworn, stating that he had been paid to go out. The deputy stated that there was nothing in the form of oath against bribery. Mr. Dargavel had a copy of the provincial Act and read the clause, and challenged and defied the deputy returning officer to put any other form of oath than the one contained in that statute. The would-be voter said that if there was going to be any row about it, he would not vote, and left the booth. But the fact is that the deputy returning officer refused point blank to submit any other oath than the one supplied by the government. The other ease is that of the postmaster who acted as deputy returning officer at Frankville, a case to which I referred the other day. This deputy returning officer refused to administer any other oath than the one supplied. And I am told that the same thing happened in many other cases. And that form of oath was supplied, I have no hesitation in saying, in order that a voter might take a bribe and then swear in his vote. And the same thing is done in Oxford and Loudon. As I have said, the telegram of the returning officer for North Oxford shows clearly that lie was of opinion that the forms of oath supplied by the government were the only ones to be used. It must be remembered that, while a .copy of the statute is sent to the returning officer, and the deputy returning officers do not look at the provincial Act or any other Act; they regard their instructions and their forms as sufficient. And I feel confident that these were prepared expressly to mislead these officers. It was the opinion throughout my riding, and, I believe, throughout the province, that the object was to omit everything that would prevent a man from being bribed and then swearing in his vote.

speechtext:
Although I have spoken once already, yet, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) has spoken a couple of times I may be allowed to say a word in order to correct myself. At first I said that I did not believe that all this was done on purpose to affect the elections in London and North Oxford, and I gave some explanation of what had happened lately in my own county. But I must say, that aifter the defence made by the minister,

and after two or three lawyers on that side have exposed their own differences in trying to explain this law, I am beginning to* think that perhaps I was wrong. Think of these differences, and then imagine a poor candidate in the province of Quebec having to fight the government in spite of this and every other disability. He has :n his county twenty-five or thirty deputy returning officers who are most active partisans and who have been working against him until the very morning of voting day; men who have never gone through the Election Act. never been instructed as to its provisions, but who are there to carry that election by every possible means. With such a law as we now have in force, and in view of what we have heard one would think that the Minister of Justice and several of his colleagues would go around to every poll and tell the deputy returning officer : ' You had better pay attention and do your duty, or there may be an action of damages against you.'
M.	O. E. TALBOT. What about the eighteen years before 1896 ?

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
I am coming to that. What we have now is all the result of the change in the law. Every Liberal I have heard on the platform has boasted that of all the promises they made thev have carried out one-they have made a change in the Franchise Act. But, now that the local governments are becoming Conservative I should not wonder if they would want to change it again. If they did so it would only be another example to prove what we already know, that their principles are not principles at all but a mere matter of opportunities. The law is not carried out at all. Every candidate should he in possession of the names of the deputy returning officers two days before the election, and these deputies should be instructed in the duties of their position. But that is not done. We can hardly even speak to the returning officer-we have to approach him with a great deal of care. And as to the deputies we are not given the names of a single one. And the same is true of the poll clerks. I have known cases where deputy returning officers were changed three times in the night before polling day. This happened in St. James division. But the hon. member for St. John and Iberville (Mr. L. O. Demers) has great consolation for us. He tells us we have a good action for damages against the deputy. That is consolation indeed, particularly when we are in opposition. Why, I caught some of my opponents in St. James division redhanded, putting bogus votes into the ballot boxes. And I had these men put in jail, but the Minister of Justice let them out. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. O. E. Talbot) speaks about the eighteen years before 1896. Before 1896 we had a Franchise Act which, while it may not have Mr. BERGERON.
been perfect was at least the same for all the provinces. To-day, every farmer carries under his arm to the polling place the form of vote he wants to take. Every provincial law must be consulted before we can know who is entitled to vote for a member of the House of Commons. And this is the reason why I believe that all this was done with a purpose. Unless you have perfectly honest. men as deputy returning officers, men who are versed in the duties of their office, it is impossible to obtain justice. Tbe law is not carried out, notwithstanding all the explanation of the Minister of Justice. The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery sends a box containing the forms, and those forms must vary according to the province.
We say :	Where are the forms ? The
deputy returning officer is an ordinary man. If he is a man of intelligence and even if he is a very honest man he is not versed in all the intricacies of what we are discussing here to-day. He says :	I have received the forms. That is the answer that my deputy returning officer gave me. He spoke to me in that way. He was an honest man. I do not believe that man wanted to do an injury to me. He said ; I have received these forms and it is my duty to administer the oaths which are incorporated in them. I read the law to him but he said : I am very sorry, but I have to follow ray instructions. I say that many of them will do the same thing even if they are honest men. Would it be any more costly or any more cumbersome to tbe government to have all of form 16 under the Ontario Act printed on the paper which is the cause of this discussion ? Why not include these two paragraphs which are the only ones making it necessary to administer the oath to the elector so as to ascertain whether he is worthy of voting, whether he is an honest man, whether he has been bribed, whether he has been bought or whether he has bought anybody ? These are the only two paragraphs of the oath that we look upon as serious. Why do anything that would suggest an error or something that is worse than an error ? Why not have the whole thing printed upon this form here or upon this for the province of Quebec ? Why not mark it or write it and say this form is part of the provincial Act and part of the Dominion Act, but it only makes one form of oath for the elector to take ? 1 wanted to give some explanation of what I said before. I have done it because I am commencing to be convinced that there is a design in this. It is done in a very clever way. Elections have been going on to-day in two constituencies. All of these deputy returning officers are politicians. They are strong friends of hon. gentlemen opposite and even if they are honest men, if there is any doubt it will be decided in favour of the government candidate. If there is one thing more than another that we are all interested in it is that elections should

be impartially and honestly carried on in this country.
