speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bergeron) who has just taken his seat has been referring to the difficulties the poor candidates who are now running in the Conservative interest in the province of Quebec have to face in order to get returned, and he says that the returning officers have been suspected of not being disposed to give them fair-play. I ask him how elections were carried out during the 18 years previous to 1896 ?	1 will not
make a speech about it, but I will just mention a certain instance and quote the law in order to show the difficulties we also had to meet under the law as it was then in existence. I remember that in 1893, in the parish of Ste. l'erpetue, in L'Islet county, 27 voters were disfranchised. Why ? They had a form of oath in the law then in existence. Form X, paragraph 2, which read as follows : ,
That my application to have my name so registered was refused ; that I have duly appealed from such decision of the said revising officer, pursuant to the provisions of the said Act.
It was then understood and agreed that if a man's name was not on the list, if that man took an oath that his name should have been on the list, provided he made his application in time, if his application were not accepted, he had the right to vote, but there was nothing to cover the case of the voter whose name had been placed on the list but which had been stricken oil by the paid heelers of the party, and I remember that at this particular poll, 27 good Liberals were disfranchised because there was not an oath which would apply to them. Yet, here is the hon. member for Beauharnois rising in his place as the representative of the party of purity of those days, but forgetting the difficulties against which we had to contend for 18 years. .Up to 1896 we had to follow the salaried officers of t he former government from parish to parish in order to endeavour to secure fair-play for the people and to see that not only the names of Liberals, but those of Conservatives who were entitled to vote were put on the list. I remember that for three weeks I followed a salaried officer of the government in the province of Quebec to see that the people got fair-play. I spent $350 of my own money to see that fair-play was given to the people, but when the lists were issued we found that the names of 375 voters had been stricken off the list although they had formerly been put on the list. These are the things we had to fight against up to 1896, and I think it is with very bad grace that these hon. gentlemen opposite now find fault with the condition of things prevailing at the present time.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
If I may be permitted to say one or two words in reply to what 234
has fallen from my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) I would like to do so. The object of the Dominion Elections Act, 1900, was obviously to make plain to the returning officers throughout the country what form of oath should be used. It was absolutely necessary that the form should be made plain, because you were using the provincial forms which varied according to the different provinces, and you were also providing for certain purposes a form for use throughout the whole of Canada. You therefore had a form of oath which varied in each province but a portion of which was the same throughout Canada. It would seem obvious that under these circumstances the provisions of section 21 of the statute should be followed strictly, and I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is able to argue that they have been followed strictly. I will point out why I think that. Section 21 provides that the returning officer-omitting matters that are immaterial-should receive a copy of the Act, the instructions approved by the Governor in Council and the forms of oath referred to in sections 65, 66 and 68. These are the three essentials as to the information which should be given to the returning officer for the purpose of carrying on the election. Now, we come to section 65. Section 65 says that the voter

Shall, before receiving his ballot paper, take such oath of qualification as by the law of the province he may in the like case at a provincial election be required to take, such changes having been made in the form of oath as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice says that only part of the oath prescribed by the provincial Act is the oath of qualification. The statute speaks of the oath of qualification not such part of the oath as relates to qualification. The statute provides that he shall:
-take such oath of qualification as by the law of the province he may in ihe like ease at a provincial election be required to take, such changes having been made in the form of oath as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held, and shall' also, if so required, take the oath in Form ' U.'
The elector may be required to take the provincial oath of qualification and also to take the oath in Form 1 U If the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice were a correct argument he would have to admit that the form sent out in 1904 is an incorrect form, because it contains the provision which is embodied in both the provincial form and the Dominion form ; that is to say that the government sent out to the returning officers in the month of November last a form of oath which contains these words :
That you have not voted before at this election, either at this or any other polling place.

The Minister of Justice seems to think that anything that had been provided for in Form ' U ' must be omitted from the provincial form. You have there exactly a provision contained in Form ' U.'

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: In the provincial statutes there is a definition of what bribery is and there is also a definition in the federal statute. Then, if we are going to adopt the oath as it is incorporated in the provincial law, we should have the elector declaring whether he has been guilty of corrupt practices under the provincial laws. That is certainly not the intention of parliament because our law provided for the declaration of the corrupt practice.

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brodeur) has not observed the words I read :
Such changes having been made in the form of oath to make it applicable to the election being held.	.
I was dealing with the point on which the Minister of Justice rested his case : that the provincial oath is an oath of qualification, and the oath in Form ' TJ ' is not an oath of qualification. The argument which says that whatever is in one oath should be eliminated from the other, would demonstrate absolutely that the form of oath sent out in 1904 is wrong, because it contains a provision which is also found in Form ' U.' The essential point about the whole matter is this : that you are to send out the forms. The Minister of Justice says they have sent out the forms, and he refers us to the instructions, and the instructions are in these words :
The oaths prescribed under sections 64, 65, 74 and 75, Forms ' T,' ' U,' ' V,' * W,' first schedule, are administered viva voce. You will instruct your deputies that, when occasion demands it, they will swear the elector direct from the copy of the Dominion Elections Act which is supplied to them.
Forms of the other oaths prescribed by the provincial law, adapted to the purposes of the present election, are furnished to you herewith.
That is not what the statute says. The statute does not say the forms of the other oaths prescribed by the provincial law are to be sent herewith. The statute says :
The instructions referred to in subsection 1 of this section shall contain forms of the oath referred to in sections 65, 66 and 68.
And that, for the very reason that because you have adapted to Dominion purposes oaths contained in provincial Acts ; because you are also supplying a certain form applicable to all the provinces under the Dominion Elections Act, the statute makes it absolutely necessary that the exact form for each province should be sent forward to each deputy returning officer. The way the matter has worked out shows the absolute necessity for that. If the statute intended that, it was wise, and

maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
in no other way can you work it out satisfactorily, as has been shown by the practical experience of lion, gentlemen in this House.
If you leave the deputy returning officer to work this out for himself under the form of instructions the Minister of Justice has referred to, you will have exactly the same difficulty which prevailed in nearly every electoral district in this country. You have adopted an extraordinary procedure ; you have adopted, not only the provincial voters' lists, but part at least of the provincial form of oath. You have added to that the Dominion form of oath, and it is essential therefore, when you put your instructions in the hands of the returning officer, that you shall make them so absolutely plain to him that any man reading the instructions 'and reading the forms will know exactly what to do. We complain that you sent a form to the returning officers which some returning officers at least ciaimed to he an exclusive form. Every line and every word of these instructions will not be present to the mind of a deputy returning officer when he is carrying on an election in the hurry and confusion and controversy that sometimes arise in a polling booth. But if you have a form placed before him which contains everything that any voter can be required to swear to when be comes to vote, then you will not have the difficulty that has occurred. It may be that a very intelligent and studious returning officer, or deputy returning officer, if he cut out from the Dominion statutes what was necessary and added it to the form placed before him, might get along all right; but this statute was designed to give him a form -which, when he had it before him, would guide him exactly in the course which the law intended. Notwithstanding the argument of the Minister of Justice, I venture the statement that the forms which have been sent out are misleading ; that they are not the forms which are contemplated by the statute ; that the intention was that the forms sent forward with the instructions would contain everything that the deputy returning officer would be required to administer to auy voter. Whether I am right in that or not, I am sincerely of that opinion, and X venture to think that the Minister of Justice, after what lie has heard to-day, will conclude that that would be a wise way to carry out the law. If the law does not mean that at present, then the law should he amended in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO RETURNING OFFICERS IN BY-ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I think I should make a statement to the House. The im-piession may have gone abroad that the Secretary of State is responsible for these forms as they went out. I sent for Mr. Fraser, who acted as Deputy Minister of Justice in the absence of Mr. Neweombe, and he tells me that I am responsible. Mr. Fraser prepared a memorandum for me on the 23rd of August, 1903, suggesting this

change, and I approved of it. Therefore, I should take the responsibility for the same.
Sir WILFRID LAURIE®. If I may be permitted one more word, I would say that we know a little more of what has taken place in these elections that have just been concluded, and the result of which we shall know presently, than we knew when my hen. friend (Mr. Armstrong) brought the question to the attention of the House. I concluded from the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) that it would not have been possible for an elector to be sworn to-day as to whether or not he had accepted a bribe in contravention of the law. We now know that such is not the case. It was open to any elector to challenge the vote of any other elector and to put to him the oath as to whether or not he .had received a bribe and was disqualified. That is now beyond doubt, because, although the form that was used in 1900 has been amended by striking cut .paragraphs 8 and 9, which refer to bribery in the province of Ontario, the returning officer was supplied with a form of oath to be administered to the voter, which is contained in Form ' U,' and which is :
You swear or solemnly affirm

That you have not been disfranchised under the provisions of the Act to disfranchise voters who have taken bribes, or for corrupt practices, under the Dominion Elections Act, 1900.
That you have not voted before at this election, either at this or at any other polling place;	*
That you have not received anything, that you do not expect anything, nor has anything been promised you directly or indirectly, to induce you to vote at this election, either for loss of time, travelling expenses, hire of team, or for any other services connected therewith ;
That you have not directly or indirectly paid or promised anything to any person either to induce him to vote or to refrain from voting at this election ;
That you are not otherwise disqualified from voting at this election.
This is as broad as the oath under the Ontario law, aud therefore no injustice could have been done to any one. I would say further that these very forms were used iu the elections in November, 1904, and, although seven months have elapsed since that time, I have not heard that any particular injustice has been done to anybody. My hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) says that he could not have this form with regard to bribery used in his election. That may be, but I do not know of any election in which you do not hear some complaint that there has been an irregularity. Even in the forms used for the ballots irregularities have been committed, aud committed most innocently. There is the Wentworth election case, now before the Supreme Court, where forty voters were disfranchised by an act of the returning officer, and, had they not been disfranchised, the Liberal candidate would have beeu returned. That cannot have 2341
beeu done in bad faith, because if the returning officer in Wentworth was a political partisan, as It is said he was, it was his own party which suffered. I quite agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition aud with everybody else who has spoken on that side, that we should endeavour to make the law as simple as possible ; and if we have printed forms of oaths to distribute, perhaps it would be less confusing to the returning officers if the other forms in this book were included. If that is a proper suggestion, I have no doubt the government would be anxious to have it carried out; and for my part I shall be glad to bring the matter at once to the attention of the Secretary of State. Because the returning officers are partisans, it does not follow that they are dishonest; on the contrary, I believe they are honest men, who desire to do justice. But as these laws are only brought into operation once in four or five years, they are liable to be forgotten ; so that the simpler the forms are the better. Certainly the Minister of Justice has no objection to having the matter attended to ; and he has thrown out the excellent suggestion that it he referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections, where it can be threshed out, and where members on both sides of the House can give their opinions. For my part, I would be glad to act on this suggestion if it is agreeable to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
Might I ask the Minister of Justice what is the reason we did not establish a general form of oath when we passed the Act ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because there are different qualifications in the various provinces. After having listened to the discussion, I think myself that the instructions to the returning officers should, in the spirit of the Act, contain every form of oath, instead of referring to an oath in the Franchise Act or in any other Act, as at present. Every form of oath should be embodied in instructions themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to hear the hon. Minister of Justice make that remark. After the discussion which has taken place, I think it must be admitted that the Prime Minister's rebuke to me was quite uncalled for. I can only say that I believe I was doing my duty in bringing this matter before the House and the country. If the form of oath is not satisfactory, is it not wise for us to change it and make it satisfactory ? I might also say, with regard to notifying the government, that I did what I could in that respect. I went to the returning officer and urged upon him the necessity of adding to the form which he had sent out to the deputies, these clauses which we have been discussing this afternoon. In doing that I believe that I was doing what was right; and I think the argument here

this afternoon proves that it would have been wise had these two sections been added. You cannot expect men throughout the country to pick out of the Acts what is suitable for the occasion. I sincerely hope that before long the Minister of Justice will see that the forms sent out in future shall have these bribery clauses included. When the right lion. Prime Minister says that the government is not responsible, I cannot agree with liiin.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that ; I say we are responsible.

I am very glad to hear it. I understood the right hon. gentleman to say that the government were not responsible for the present situation. However, so far as our judgment goes on this side of the House, this oath, as it has been administered, is to a certain extent a mutilated oath, and I hope the time is not far distant when the government will arrange to have these forms sent out in a proper way.

BRODEUR-(for Minister of Public Works). This is to continue the heavy repairs which were begun in the spring of 1004. The expenditures from the 1st of July to 31st December, 1904, was $2,985.83. This will complete the work.
Ottawa river-wharf near the mouth of Riviere du Lievre, $4,500.

This is to make further provision for the construction of a public work at Masson or Buckingham Junction, some 20 miles below Ottawa, so as to give shipping faiicilities. It is government property. The total estimate is $S,500 and this $4,500 will complete.

What is the policy of the government with regard to building wharfs ? They seem to favour some particular places and utterly ignore others. We have never had a wharf built by the government in the riding I represent. Would the minister state what are the conditions which will induce the government to build a wharf ?
The policy is the same as that which was carried on by our predecessors, namely, to construct wharfs for the accommodation of the public where the public interest demands it.

We should have something more definite. Because the Conservative government set the example is no reason why this government should follow it. If wharfs are to be built indiscriminately, without regard to any definite plan or condition or policy, you will have people in every locality asking the government to build their wharfs. Why should not these works be left to private enterprise ? In the part of the country where I come from, the wharfs are built by private individuals, but I do not see why we should not have them built by the government, if the government is to follow the policy of building them wherever the pressure is strong enough to influence it.

It is the duty of the government to see that shipping facilities are given wherever they are required for the development of trade. There are localities where private enterprise will do the work. On the Ottawa river there are wharfs which have been built by private companies, but these companies will not allow the public to use them and exercise a monopoly over them. It is thus frequently found advisable in the public interest, in order to afford shipping facilities to the whole community, that the government should construct these works.

I think the first reason the hon. gentleman gave is the best one, and that is that he is following the example of his predecessor. But lie evidently forgets that his party, when in opposition, took days and days to criticise these expenditures by the late government. Evidently they were not sincere in ,their criticisms' since they say_they are carrying out the same policy.

At that place ?

At this place ; it was the
first time the dredging was done. This is on
the Richelieu river between Lake Champlain and Chambly.

I am informed it is intended to put tvyo dredges if we can find another one.

This $7,000 will not go far. Is there to be a vote in the supplementary estimates 7

The chief engineer informs me that $7,000 will cover the work that will he done this season.
Riviere St. Louis-feeders-opening waterways between Ste. Anicet and Ste. Barbe, $10,-
000.

This vote is asked to carry on projected improvements at the head of Riviere St. Louis with a view to securing an outlet for drainage waters and so preventing the rising of Lake St. Francis as a result of the dams built in 1840 toy the united provinces of Upper and Lower Canada at the head of the Beauharnois canal.
Is that work going on 7
No work has been done. That is why we are asking a revote of the whole amount.
Was work done there in the fall of 1904 7
There was some work done for a few weeks.
About what time of the year 7
The expenditure was from 1st July to 1st December-I have no more definite date.
Is it not a fact that only a few men were on that work about the latter part of October and early in November 7
That may be ; I do not know.
What work is to be done 7

As I have explained, the government intend to secure an outlet for the water which, coming from the St. Lawrence now overflows the land in that locality. The people there claim-aud it would seem that their contention is correct though I have no information on the subject myself -that this overflow has been caused by the action of the government. So, this money is voted to prevent the repetition of this overflow. I am sure the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Walsh) will not object to the expenditure.
I would like to know where the $5,000 was spent ?
It was only $500.
In 1904-5 there was a vote of $15,000, and I see now that there is a revote of only $10,000.

The estimates before us were prepared about the beginning of January, and it was expected that a certaip amount of money from the vote of last year would be spent before the expiry of the fiscal year, 1st July next. That is the reason a revote of only $10,000 is asked.
I do not object to the vote but I would like to know whether the work is actually to be proceeded with ?
It is not going on at present.
But we understand that it will be prosecuted.
I do not know whether the government has taken any definite steps as to that, because we must ascertain whether the cost will not be too large.
I believe that a survey and estimate have been made ?
Yes, there was an estimate that the work would cost $99,000.

This amount for improvements at St. Louis for which $15 000 was voted last year and this item of-
St. Louis, feeders-opening waterways between St. Anicet and Ste. Barbe, $10,000.
-are as matter of fact the same work. It is a good thing and should be done. Work has been carried on here for many years. A great many works have been carried on in the River St. Louis in the last twenty-five years but they have not all been completed. My hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue understands very well that there is a good deal of politics in this.
There was.

This work lies between Huntingdon and Beauharnois which w7ere before the last election both represented by friends of the government. The government came to the conclusion that it might exercise an influence in favour of their
friends to have a certain amount of money voted for this work. Consequently $15,000 was voted for the improvements at St. Louis. The question as to the best method of doing that work was discussed for a long time. The government or the department finally came to the conclusion that it would be done better by a dredge. This is a matter in regard to which there is a difference of opinion. My own impression Is that it might be done better in another way. But, it was decided to have the work done by a dredge. Any money which was appropriated for the deepening of the river was expended on the construction of a dredge. The work of constructing the dredge was carried on until a few days before the election. They were paying one superintendent $3 a day to superintend another superintendent and so on. A few days before the election the dredge was working so hard that it broke down. After the election it was so late in the season that it had to stop work. Another $15,000 was voted for opening the waterways between St. Anicet and Ste. Barbe but my hon. friend does not know whether anything is going' on or not. The government have not made up their mind how much it will cost. I want to be more just to the government. I have no doubt that before they decided to ask parliament to vote that money they found out how much the work could be done for. I think the estimate of $96,000 is too high. If the officers of the department search the files they-will find that there is a report which was made by Mr. Parent, the engineer of the canal some years ago, in which he estimates that the work can be done for a great deal less by doing it in a different way. This is the first time I have seen the item placed in this form ' opening waterways between St. Anicet and Ste. Barbe.' Formerly it was to make a kind of dam to keep the water in Lake St. Louis.
Was there sot some work done in the old days?

There was some done but not much. It was a great deal harder to get money from the government then than it is now. This vote will go through but as Huntingdon and Beauharnois are not now represented by the same men the work will no doubt stop.

Quite the reverse. We are doing some work on the River St. Louis.
Mr.. BERGERON. On the River St. Louis you built a dredge. Unless that dredge "is put to work this money will be completely lost because she cannot be taken anywhere else. She has to stay there and unless my hon. friend places some more money in the supplementary estimates to keep that dredge at work until the end of

the season the money already spent will have been spent in an almost useless way. I think it is very important that some work should be done between Anicet and Ste. Bartoe. My bon. friend, I am sure, will find that the amount of money which he has mentioned there is necessary, but before the government asked parliament to vote $15,000 for that part of the work they surely must have had an idea of how much it would cost, and they must know that the Work there was promised to be done. It was promised by Mr. Boy and his friends and it was promised by the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) very often in my presence. It is a good work, it should be done and I call upon my hon. friend to see that the money which is voted is spent in prosecuting this work to as great an extent as possible.
Mr. B'RODEUR. I do not know why my hon. friend should complain so much of the action of the government. The money has been voted. He says that he was eighteen years asking for the money to do this work and that he could not get it ; yet, because we have begun the work and because we have begun the construction of a dredge which was absolutely necessary, my hon. friend complains. He suggests another way of doing the work. I would like to know what other way-toy pick and shovel?
Yes.

I think it will be much more expensive than to do the work by dredging even if the dredge could be used only in that place. It is a work which will cost some money and I think that if the work were done by pick and shovel it would not be done as satisfactorily as it would be done toy a dredge to say nothing of the fact that it would cost a great deal more. My hon. friend should not complain of the fact that the late member succeeded in having money voted for this work after my hon. friend had been unsuccessfully asking for it for eighteen years. If the late member was fortunate enough to have the necessary money voted for that work which he declares himself to be a very necessary work, what has my hon. friend to find fault with? Now, the work is going on. The dredge has been completed and the work will go on. The money which has been voted, I understand, will cover the expenditure ou account of that dredge during the year.

Now that the money is voted it should be expended for the object for which it is voted. I say it is a good object. If Mr. Loy were here he would not thank my hon. friend at all. That' money was promised to him about five years ago and it was put in thg estimates every year but it never amounted to anything until the election came on and Mr. Mr. BERGERON.
Loy himself has complained that he has been played upon. He has complained that the work was not done as it should have been done. This was an election promise and if my hon. friend met Mr. Loy I am sure he would tell him so himself* I cannot ask for any favour, as I have no right to ask a favour of my hon. friend.
Why not?

No, no; I would not do it. I give credit to the government that they did vote the money and I take it as an indication that they intend to have the work done although they do it very late.. The object is good.

We had $15,000 voted last year and more than $S,000 has been already spent.
Mr. BERGERON But you expended it upon the construction of a dredge. There is no work done yet.

But, it is in connection with that work. I do not know why my hon. friend should complain because he admits that the dredge could be used only there. The dredge has been built for that purpose and it is beginning the work about which my hon. friend should not complain at all.
Why did the dredge not begin to work until May? She is not doing anything now, I understand.

Because it was not completed.
Mr. BERGERON, if was completed last fall.
That is not the information I have.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if any work is going ou there. The only work which has been done there was done by this pick and shovel brigade which you speak of. just before the last election. A few men were set at work before polling day.
If there is too much complaint about the pick and shovel brigade I will drop the item pure and simple. Stands.

I do not know tuat we should allow this item to stand. The hon. minister is not running the whole House. There is no use of getting mad because we choose to criticise an item. I think the hon. minister had better keep his temper.
I am keeping my temper.

Because a member from that section of the country chooses to offer a little fair criticism I think the

hon. minister is not doing justice to his usual reputation in this House bv standing up and threatening to drop the item.
We will consider it.

I will give the Minister of Inland Revenue the credit of being courteous generally, but lie made a mistake in attacking my young friend (Mr. Walsh) and threatening to drop this item. The minister can suit himself about dropping the item, but he should not drop it because a member on this side thought it his duty to offer reasonable criticism.

If the minister had allowed me to finish my explanation, he would have understood my position. The work was promised by friends of the government, and I have no criticism as to that, but the men whose property is affected came to the conclusion that the work was not to be prosecuted, and they asked me (a great many times to inquire about it. That was my object in mentioning the matter. Personally,
I have no interest, 'but the people there have been promised it for years and they are interested. Nothing has been done to proceed with the work this year, and that is why I asked what was the intention of the government.

I object to this further example of the very improper method in which the government deals with these matters. Last year $15,000 was granted for this work ; apparently a small sum was expended, and the minister tells us that up to the 1st of July next $5,000 will have been expended, and he asks a revote of $10,000. It transpires that the minister has an estimate of what this work is going to cost, which he says amounts to $96,000, but he says that estimate is an exaggeration.
I said the estimate was $96,000, but I did not say it was exaggerated. That statement was made by the hon. member for Beauharnois.

I have protested time and again against taking these small votes from year to year for a work that in the end will cost a very large sum of money. I am told by hon. gentlemen on this side that this is a deserving work, but we who do not know tlie locality are entitled to be told what the entire expenditure will be without being asked to vote blindly. Some of these ex-pcndituras would never be endorsed by parliament if we knew what their ultimate cost would foe.

The excavation is estimated to cost $69,000 ; the improvements at the mouth of the river, $6,000 ; three bridges, $6,000 ; clearing of the River St. Louis, $7,000 ; and $8,000, or 10 per cent, for superintendence and contingencies. The work may be done in a way to cost less than $96000, but new surveys would have to be made for that.
Who made that report ?
Mr. Michaud, the engineer of the district.
Was there not a report made by Mr. Parent some years ago ; an entirely different report ?

The chief engineer informs me there is no record of it in the Department of Public Works, although it may be in the Department of Railways and Canals. Twenty years ago the government did work in connection with this scheme.
Does the minister gravely tell the House that $5,000 has been expended, and that he does not know what this work is going to cost ?	,
There have been only $500 spent.
The minister said $300 or $400 had been spent and that the balance of the $5,000 would be expended up to the 30th of June.

No. There was an expenditure of $548 up to the time these estimates were prepared, and it was then estimated, in January last, that $4,439 would be expended up to the 30th of June, but that money has not been expended.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why does not the minister ask for a revote of the balance of the $15,000 ?

Because the estimate had been prepared in that way, as I explained.
Mr. TAYLOR, What was the $451 spent for ?
In pick and shovel work on the land.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What work has been done for that expenditure, and why was not the balance of the vote of last year expended ? Is it the intention of the minister to discontinue the work altogether ?

I will report to the Minister of Public Works what has been said with regard to this work, and I suppose we shall have to examine the question and see whether it is advisable to continue the work or not.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said he would drop the item.
Certainly, if the member for the county wants to have the item droped.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
He did not ask to have it dropped. He was giving it fair and honest criticism, and the minister off his own bat suggested that he would drop the item. It looks as if the $15,000 was put in last year for election purposes, and now that the elec-

tion is over the minister is ready to drop the item and not go on with the work.

This work is not the same as the work I was speaking of. The object of the vote is to prevent the waters of Lake St. Francis flooding the farms of St. Anicet and Ste. Barbe. The report of Mr. Parent, an engineer of the government some years ago, recommended the building of a dam, which seems to he the more natural plan for preventing the waters of Lake St. Francis flooding these farms. The dam was partly built by the government years ago, and if it were continued, there would be no need of having waterways or bridges. That is always the idea I had of that work, and I am convinced that the figures of its cost was a great deal less than the amount mentioned by my hon. friend for the proposed work. This is a very important work, as most of these farms are valuable, and they are covered with water for a long time in the year. I was glad to see the money appropriated for this work, but why was the work not commenced in time ? We hear that a few men were there with picks and shovels; but that was not serious work, which is also evident from the fact that my hon. friend is willing to let the item stand. These are two different things, although they may both be connected with the River St. Louis. I want to hear what my hon. friend has to say before I give further criticism of the item.

The hon. member for Beauharnois evidently thinks that it would be better to proceed in some different way from that suggested in this vote. This vote is for the opening of waterways, but my hon. friend thinks it would be better to extend the dyke which was commenced some years ago, and he says there is a report of Mr. Parent to that effect. There is no such report in the Public Works Department ; but in view of the remarks of my hon. friend, I think it is the duty of the Public Works Department to look into the matter and see whether the suggestion he makes is better than what is proposed in this vote. Under the circumstances, I think it is perfectly justifiable to wait until the minister is here and can inquire into the matter and see whether it is better to adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend.

My hon. friend is not serious. I am not proposing any plan ; X am not managing the affairs of the Public Works Department; I take things as I find them. The present engineer of the department has made a report; the department have acted on that report, and have proposed a vote to parliament. I want the department to carry on their own works. I was answering my hon. friend, who said that the report mentioned the sum of $96,-
000.	I am not going to prevent my hon. friend spending that money if he wants to spend it or thinks the expenditure of it Mr. TAYLOR.
is necessary. In answer to that, I said I had seen a report in which the estimate was a great deal less, and according to which the work was to be done in a different way. The report I saw was that of an engineer, but of course I am not competent to judge between the two reports. All I ask my hon. friend is to carry out the work for which the money was voted last year. It will be childish for him to say :	we will
wait to find out whether you are not right or wrong. If he would agree to take my opinion on everything, of course let him accept this with the rest; but if he wants to leave the item out merely because I have pointed to another report, I am opposed to that.

This vote is asked for on the advice of a local engineer. My hon. friend informs me that there is another report, not in the Public Works Department but probably in the Department of Railways and Canals, because the engineer who made it was then the engineer of the latter department.

It is true that Mr. Parent was the engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals, but when I was urging the Department of Public Works to have the work done-because we have been asking to have it done for twenty-five years-that department asked Mr. Parent who was on the spot, to make a report, which he did.

The chief engineer informs me that he''never knew anything about that report of Mr. Parent, and he infers that as Mr. Parent was then the engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals, his report must be in that department. If my hon. friend however says it is in the Department of Public Works, we will look for it there. The object of the government is to drain these lands because it is complained that if they are now covered by water, that is due to some works which the government built in connection with the canal. That is why I think my hon. friend is mistaken when he says that the report must have passed through the Public Works Department.
At that time the whole thing was in the Department of Public Works.

But my hon. friend is referring to a report which was made at a time when the Public Works Department was not included in the Department of Railways and Canals. My hon. friend says that the plan we are proposing is much more expensive than that recommended in the report of Mr. Parent. Does he then think, that I would be justified, in the absence of the minister, in committing the department to an expenditure which could be reduced, if my hon. friend's statement be correct. If we can save $20,000 or $25,000 in the drain-

iug of tliose lands by the adoption of the suggestion of my hon. friend, we ought certainly to adopt it.

I am not speaking as an engineer, and I would not say that Mr. Parent's report is the better one of the two. My hon. friend should take the report of Mr. Michaud, and ask parliament to vote the money, and there will be nothing to prevent his having the work done for a less amount of money if possible. But he should not try to throw the responsibility on me if nothing should be done.	*

I am not doing that, but I say that my hon. friend is making a very valuable suggestion. He says there is a report somewhere, according to which this work may be done for less money. No money has yet been spent, why then should the government go on without looking up this other report 1

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That will not prevent my hon. friend allowing the item to pass. Then he can consult with the minister, and when we come to concurrence, if the minister thinks we ought to drop thf !tem, let him drop it. But my hon. friend should not get up in a huff and say :	Because my hon.
friend criticises, we will drop the item.

All I said was that the item should stand for the reason given by my hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron). But I am quite willing it should pass with the understanding that the minister himself will look into it.

I do not believe that the hon. minister wants to be unfair to me, especially as I am a young member. I certainly was not opposing the vote. On the contrary I wanted to know whether it is going to be expended, because we have been asking a long time to have this work done, and this waterway will have to be built some time or other.
What does my hon. friend think about a dyke ?

You will still have to make a waterway as well as a dyke. This land was flooded on account of some works erect ed at the mouth of the canal by the government, and the government recognized its obligation by paying many years ago the damages caused to some of these lands. In order to drain the lands, there must be a ditch or canal to connect with the St. Lawrence river. A dyke would not be sufficient.

Suppose a dyke would be made on the bank which would prevent the water overflowing, and that was found less expensive than a canal, does not my hon. friend think it would be better to adopt that system ?

That is not practicable because theie is a river there which flows into
the St. Lawrence, and the water is backed up this river and overflows the lands. It is necessary that a waterway be built on that account, because by closing the outlet you are preventing the water from being drained off.
Rivi6re Verte-improvements at mouth, $5,800.

This is to cover the estimated cost of completing the work commenced in 1904-5 near the mouth of the river, together with a widening and deepening of the centre of the channel, and is required to carry away the wrater of the swollen stream in the spring. The object is to prevent the properties on this side of the river being eroded by ice and currents in the spring.
Sacrd Cceur-wharf, $9,000.

This is required to complete the wharf, 210 feet long, which is being built on the north side of the Saguenay, at this place, about twelve miles above its mouth. The work is under contract.
St. Alexis, Ha Ha hay pier, $17,000.

This is also under contract. It is to complete the pier 1.44S feet long began in 1899-1900. There will be a depth of 9 to 10 feet at low water spring tide.
St. Andre de Kamouraska wharf-repairs to earth approach, &c., $6,500.

This is for the accommodation of another block of cribwork, measuring 100 feet wide, 20 feet in diameter, in order to accommodate the increasing traffic. The present structure is only 24 feet long and altogether too small for that purpose.
Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere-reconstruction of pier. $1,200.
This is to cover the estimated cost of rebuilding the pier which wa s destroyed in 1905.
What county is that in ?

Kamouraska.
St. Chairles BorromOe-wharf, $4,000.

This vote is asked in order to make further provision towards the construction of a small wharf. It is in the county of Chicoutimi.
Ste. Famille, Island of Orleans-extension of wharf, $700.
Is that a new wharf ? Mr. BRODEUR. It is an old work.
When was it built ? Mr. BRODEUR. About twenty years ago. Mr. BARKER. Will this complete the work ?

Yes.
Ste. Fid61e wharf, $11,000.
This is to complete the payments for 1906 in connection with the public works being built at Ste. Fidele in Charlevois.
Will that complete the work ?
Yes, it is expected to complete it.
Is that the estimate given to the department that it will complete ?
Yes, according to the estimate of the department.
$3,000 was voted before which will make $14,000 in all.

Yes.
St. Francois, Island of Orleans-approach to isolated block, $10,000.	.

This is to make provision for the construction of a length of 200 feet of cribwork to the isolated block. It stands at a distance of 650 feet from high water mark. It is proposed to call for tenders. This is in Montmorency county.
That is a revote ?

The department had no time to prepare plans last fall. The plans are being prepared now.
St. Francois de Sales-wharf, &c., on River James, $7,000.
This is to make provision for the construction of a block from the river.
Why was that not expended last year ?
I understand the department had no time to prepare the plans.

There are four items here, one after the other all in the same position, money granted last year and not a dollar has been spent. These grants were made two or three months before the elections. I think the inference is fair, it was all done in August or July, preparatory to the autumn elections, and not a dollar was spent, and now the government come back this year for renewals of these votes.

My hon. friend is mistaken. For most of the works for which money was voted last year the plans were prepared. Parliament prorogued late and it was not known before the appropriation was voted whether the money would be at the disposal of the department or not. I must mention the fact-I do not know for what reason the criticism is made-but in my district there was a public building in which I was much interested, it was of the greatest importance to me that the work should be done, but I could not get the plans prepared. The officers of the depar-ment did their best, they worked day and night upon different works for which money was voted, but the money having been voted so late in some cases the plans could not be prepared.
And the electors were allowed to live in expectation.
I do not think this had anything to do

No ?
Mr. BRODEUR

with the election. And
I am sure the member for Laval (Mr. Leonard) will not say that.
Are plans prepared during the winter ?
They are being prepared now.
The department took a grant before the first of July for this money?

Are they ready ? have had a whole year.
You
No, it was after July 1st that parliament prorogued.
A month afterwards. Was nothing done last year, was no estimate made ?
Nothing has been done, no.
Was there any reason for granting it last year when it was known the work could not be done ?
It was expected the work would be done last year, but the plans could not be prepared.
Had the November elections anything to do with it ?
It is true the elections were held then, but we might expect the plans could be prepared ; there were manv works to be carried on.

They are just about ready.
St. Fuljrence wharf, $5,000.
This covers the estimated cost of extending the block and span high water wharf commenced in 1904 on the north side of the River Saguenay, 10 miles below Chicoutimi.
Will this complete that work ?
Y'es.
The estimate given to the government shows that this $5,000 will complete the work ?

Yes.
St. Gedeon Islands-wharf, $2,500.

This work is under contract, it is to complete.

St. Jean, Island of Orleans-repairs to wharf, $5,000.
What county is this in ?
Montmorency.
I would like to inquire if the iirovincial government is called upon to give any share of the expense for the construction of these works ?
No, they are public property. It is repairs made to a wharf which belongs to the government.

The reason I asked was that in the River St. John, New Brunswick there is an amount here :
To provide for contributions to local government, not to exceed one-half the first cost of wharfs built by them in tidal waters.
I understand that is in virtue of an understanding between two governments.
I should think a similar understanding should be made in both cases.
These are inland waters, I understand ; but the present work is on the River St. Lawrence.
The River St. John is a t cry important river.
The St. John is a navigable river, as the St. Lawrence is.
Is it of as much importance ?

No ; but the same principle applies.
Mr. BRODEUR, This work was built many years ago, and the vote is only for repairs.

I am not complaining of this expenditure, but I think that if the Dominion government build wharfs on the St Lawrence, they ought to build them on other waters.
St. Simeon wharf-extension, $15,500.
This is under contract.
What is the nature of the work ?

This is to complete the work in connection with the approach to the isolated pier at St. Simeon, which is being-built under contract, The amount of the contract is $19,062.67, and the contractor is Napoleon Trudel.
How many tenders were there ?	[DOT]

I have not that information, but I can get it if the hon. gentleman desires. The tenders were advertised for
publicly, and the contract was given to the lowest tenderer.
Terrebonne-wharf with approach, on River Jesus, $7,000.
Are the plans ready for this ?
They are being made ready. It is just the same case as the other.

(Translation.) Are those works being carried out simultaneously with those that are in process at St. Francis of Sales for which a vote has just been taken ?
Mr. BRODEUR, (Translation.) Altnougb the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Walsh) does not seem to take any stock in the statement made by the government when asking a vote from the House in connection with such works, I may tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Leonard) that they will be carried out in the proper time. I am quite sure that the works at St. Francis of Sales will be dealt with in the same way as those at Terrebonne which have just been referred to.

(Translation.) I do not find any fault with ihe works contemplated here; on the contrary, i believe that they will serve a useful purpose. I entertain no doubt about their being carried out, owing to the fact that both the county of Terrebonne and that of Laval will be benefited by those works.
(Translation.) Those works concern not only the county of Terrebonne, but also two other constituencies. They will prove useful to the three counties of Laval, Terrebonne and L'Assomption.

(Translation.) As I said a little while ago, I find no fault with the contemplated works ; but I wanted to know whether they were to be carried out this year, and whether the government intended to redeem a promise made long ago.
Yamaska river-dredging, $10,000.
This is under contract.
Who has the contract ?
William Davis & Son, of Ottawa. This is dredging at the mouth of the River Yamaska, which empties into the St. Lawrence. The work has been going on for some time.
What is the object of this work ?
It is at the mouth of the river and allows navigation of the Yamaska, which is navigable for several miles above this place.

Is it not true that there are certain saw-mills on the Yamaska, and that this work is done to benefit these mills, and should be done by private enterprise rather than at the expense of the country ?

Mi\ BRODEUR. No ; there are no mills there that I know of, and I know the place very well.
What vessels ply there- ocean steamers ?
No, but market boats running between places on the river and Sorel.	.
It seems to me the same argument that would justify this work would justify work on the St. John. If the Yamaska empties into the St. Lawrence, the St. John empties into the Bay of Fundy.
I think that dredging in New Brunswick is done by the government.
Only in the harbours, not in tributaries of the St. John.
I am informed that there were two dredges working on tributaries of the St. John last year.
Did we not vote some money in the supplementary estimates for this dredging at the mouth of the Yamaska ?
Yes ; $12,200 has been spent so far. It must have been $2,000 that was voted in the supplementary estimates. I have not the figures before me.
What is the material that is taken out ?

county in which the proposed work is, the purpose for which it is required, the amount that is already expended, the total amount that is estimated for the completion of the work, and the probable date of completion in each instance. RORpen. Will that complete the work?

In Guysborough county.

ROI1DEN. That seems to be a very large amount for a mere boat landing.

North Victoria.

40,000	tons. They have been developing during the winter and the intended output during the coming season is about 1,000 tons per day.

This is a new company called the Gowrie Blockhouse Collieries.
Developing a new seam ?

The Dominion Coal Company have abandoned the piers at Cow bay. This colliei'y company have no connection with the railways, and are entirely dependent on their own wharf for the shipment of their coal. They have erected a short distance from this breakwater a pier, and this breakwater will protect that pier. They cannot build their pier .sufficiently large to accommodate their traffic until the breakwater is restored to its former condition. The work on Cow bay is a very old work on which twenty years ago or more a very large amount of money was expended. Ten or twelve years ago about 200 feet of that breakwater was carried away, and nothing was done to save it. The result has been that during the last eight or nine years a large amount of money has had to be expended to preserve what remained of that work. What did remain has been jxre-served and is in fairly good condition now ; but in order that the breakwater may become useful to the port, it is necessary that it should be restored. The coal company cannot carry on their work unless the breakwater is restored.
What is the total quantity of coal supposed to be in the seam that is being developed ? Will it continue at the rate of 1,000 tons a day for any great length of time ?
\res. There are millions and millions of tons of coal in the area held by these people.
Is the seam under the Archibald seam ?
Yes, and their property is a submarine area. They have now reached their own property, and last year they drove their levels in order to get a considerable output this season.
It amounts, I suppose. to building a shipping place for this company ? I do not say that may not be justifiable.

I am perfectly willing to admit that it is the most important purpose that this breakwater will serve. At the same time, I desire to call the attention of the committee to the fact that Cow bay is a very important fishing community, and the people who have fishing craft are entirely dependent oh the breakwater for the safety of their waft. The present coal company are not using the breakwater for the purposes of their own shipment. They are erecting their own pier
at a very considerable expense ; but this breakwater is necessary to protect it.
In other words, the breakwater forms a harbour, and it is to be put in the same position for this company that it was for the Archibald company years ago ?
Precisely so.
I would ask the minister to give us the details of the $225,000 that this work is likely to cost. What are the different portions of the expenditure ?

To construct and complete the dock removing the ballast deposit along the inner quay face and placing concrete blocks or quarried stone on seaward face and outer end of portion of breakwater still standing, $89,700 ; restoring the breakwater to its original length by constructing 260 feet of native timber cribwork filled with concrete placed along the continuation of the inner face of the work, and protecting with concrete blocks or quarried stone the seaward side of the proposed extension, $135,800.

front of 20 feet, mean depth 129 feet. This is the estimated cost.

Mr. BROI>EUR. This is to provide for the construction of an approach 700 feet long, 20 feet wide. It is in Halifax county and the total cost will be $2,000.

Inverness (Broad cove) Mines harbour-repairs to harbour works, $10,000.
This is for the extension of the harbour works built by the Inverness Coal Company. The total cost will be $10,000. The work will not be started until the property is transferred to the Crown.
How is it that a harbour on which you propose to spend money can be private property ?

We are having it transferred to the Crown because if it were left in the hands of a private corporation, that company would have the monopoly and could prevent others using it. It belongs now to the Inverness Railway and Coal Company.
Mr. OSLER, This is to provide the coal company with a wharf and get the government to spend $10,000 on it ?	[DOT]

It will be transferred to the government.
Mr. OSIjER. Why should the government take it over ?
In order to give the general public the use of it.

I am interested in some shipping in Lake Ontario in connection with the Niagara Navigation Company. We have had to build our own wharf. We have to keep it in repair. Other people must have a public wharf more or less and if the government are doing this it would be a good thing to transfer the wharf and get the government to keep it up.
The company would then be willing to pay wharfage dues ?

Certainly, if the government would take charge of it. On the face of it, this looks like a private wharf, owned by a Private company, which is getting the government to relieve them from the responsibility of keeping it up ; and they make it a public wharf, the company getting the full benefit of it as they do now.

I have a case in mind where a private company absolutely refused to transfer the wharf unless they got private use of it ; they would not allow the public to use the work as they chose. I do not know whether it would be good policy for the government to take over all the
works, but I suppose where it is for the public advantage it should be done.
What other necessity is there for this work 5

The Inverness Coal Company agreed with the government to hand them over this harbour in the interests of the public, provided that parliament would make a grant in behalf of that harbour, in order that it would be improved to accommodate the public. There is. now a town of about 3,000 inhabitants that has sprung up around that mine and in the vicinity of that harbour. The present company purchased these works from the original company who used them, but the present company have built a railway for their own purposes, and ships their coal at the Strait of Canso ; they have abandoned this harbour and these works altogether, so that it is the public that is now interested in the repair and fixing up of this harbour for public use.
Is it an artificial harbour ?

It was a large pond-a small lake, in fact-and the original company that owned the mines cut a narrow isthmus that existed between this small lake and the sea and built two piers to protect the entrance to this harbour, and used it in a small way to make small shipments of coal when they were first developing that coal property, but they sold out to the present company, who built their own rail-way to ship from the Strait of Canso, where they now have one of the finest shipping places perhaps in North America ; it is just as good and extensive a shipping place as that of the Dominion Coal Company in Sydney, and they thus have no use whatever for the Broad Cove harbour, as it was formerly called. I say again it Is the public that are interested in opening up this harbour, a considerable business having sprung up around the mines. The public are thus interested in the opening up of this harbour and having it for use, in order that the business interests of the place may be encouraged, particularly that a fair amount of competition may be set up with the company's railway, running-sixty miles, over which almost every article of consumption for that town must be carried.
What is the nature of the work ; completing piers, dredging the harbour, deepening the channel, or what ?

There are two piers built for the protection of the entrance to the harbour, in other words, to keep sand from being banked up at the entrance of the harbour. These piers have been wrecked by storms from time to time, and the company at present owning them, having no particular interest in maintaining them, allowed them to go to wreck, and the object of the gov-

eminent now. in the public interest, is to keep the company to the original engagement, that is to hand the harbour and these old works over to the public on condition that the government would rebuild those piers and otherwise render the harbour fit for shipping purposes. There is no doubt the company would use the harbour for local shipping of their coal in a small way to local ports as well as the public, but the government would not make a grant without the company first arranging to hand over the harbour to the public. The company are now hesitating to hand these works over, and untii they do so the government refused to go on with the work, -and the prospects are that the entrance to that har-hour will very likely have to be expropriated by the government in the public interest, in order that this grant may be used for the purpose for which it was voted.

When the piers are built, will they be covered by the company with tracks and constructions of various kinds for handling the coal, so that the companv would have a practical monopoly of the use of this harbour ?
Oh, no ; they are simply brush and stone for the protection of the entrance to the harbour. The facilities for handling the coal are entirely within the harbour.
What is the total amount ?
It is understood that before the government spends this money they will have handed over this Inside harbour that the member for Inverness speaks of ?
That, as I understand, is a condition precedent to the expenditure of the money.
That is the reason no expenditure has been made.
The member for Inves-nciss said the government would have to expropriate it.
Unless the company v.ould keep up to their promise.
I understand the owners have agreed to transfer.
The money should be voted provisionally that no share of it would be spent in purchasing property.
The committee may be sure that no money will be spent unless a transfer is made to the government.
That is, all the money is to be spent on work ?
Yes.

There are no payments for property ?

No.

I think it is very much like the case of the harbour at Glace Bay last year, where some money was voted on the understanding it was not to be expended until the harbour to be converted into a public harbour should be transferred from the company. In that case, as in this, the harbour had been created, and it was practically an artificial harbour, used entirely for the purposes of a corporation and controlled by that corporation. The promise then made to the committee was, and the one I understand that is being made nows is, that the money will not be expended unless there is such a transfer as will make the hrrbour available in every way for the public use, so that it will cease to be a private harbour or private work, and will become, to all intents and purposes, a public harbour, just the same as if it had been a public harbour from the commencement. Janvrin's island wharf, $600.
This vote is to complete the wharf on the north side of this island. To complete it will cost $600.

What has been spent so far ?
- Mr. BRODEUR. $2,000 has been expended and $600 is required to complete.
What county is this ?

We want to know what the additional work that you are to do is ?

Is it under contract?

This is in the county of Richmond.

How much will be the total cost?
An examination will be made, and if the work can be done for $1,000 it will be done.

Yes.
What county is it in? '

Inverness.

At last ?
This is a revote and it is to carry out the work of improving Lunenburg harbour in accordance with the estimate, which is $8,000.
Will the money be spent this year?

speechtext: Y'ou would have as good a chance to find it there as anvwhere else.
Perhaps the Minister of Justice would give his views on the subject.

The British North America Act, 1867, provides that the public works and property of each province enumerated in schedule 3, shall be the property of Canada. Schedule 3 specifies these works to be: Canals, and waterpowers connected therewith, lighthouses and piers Sable Island, and public harbours. The harbour of Port Hood is on the west coast of Cape Breton island, about twenty miles to the northward of the northern entrance to the Strait of Canso.
The harbour was formerly <a secure one, Smith island, which forms its west side, having been connected with the mainland by a range of sand hills. In 1893 the sea made a breach through this protection ; the opening, at first narrow, was enlarged by the tidal currents with increasing rapidity until it was entirely swept away. The harbour is now unsafe during northerly gales, except in a small cove on the east side of Smith island.
In March, 1902, a report was submitted on the closing of the northern entrance in which the estimated cost of work suggested varied from $482,000 to $291,000, according to design and location.
